                           OVERSIGHT FINDINGS

    With respect to clause 3(c)(1) of rule XIII of the Rules of 
the House of Representatives, this legislation results from 
hearings and other oversight activities conducted by the 
committee pursuant to clause 2(b)(1) of rule X. The findings 
are reflected in the body of this report.

                GENERAL PERFORMANCE GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

    With respect to clause 3(c)(4) of rule XIII of the Rules of 
the House of Representatives, the general goals and objectives 
of H.R. 8800 are to maintain the national defense, to prepare 
the United States to meet current and future challenges to the 
national defense, and to accomplish each of those goals and 
objectives in a responsible manner.
    The bill authorizes $1.14 trillion of discretionary funding 
to support national defense requirements. The bill authorizes 
funding sufficient to provide a 5 to 7 percent pay raise for 
servicemembers, to invest in key maintenance and readiness 
areas, and to modernize the force to deter adversaries.
    The bill continues the longstanding work of the Committee 
on Armed Services to provide U.S. military forces with 
sufficient resources to maintain the national defense, and it 
fulfills the committee's duties under Article I, Section 8, of 
the Constitution.

                     STATEMENT OF FEDERAL MANDATES

    The committee adopts as its own the estimate of Federal 
mandates prepared by the Director of the Congressional Budget 
Office pursuant to section 423 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform 
Act.

                  FEDERAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE STATEMENT

    Consistent with the requirements of section 5(b) of the 
Federal Advisory Committee Act, the committee finds that the 
functions of the proposed advisory committees authorized in the 
bill are not currently being performed, nor could they be 
performed, by one or more agencies, an advisory committee 
already in existence, or by enlarging the mandate of an 
existing advisory committee.

                APPLICABILITY TO THE LEGISLATIVE BRANCH

    The committee finds that this legislation does not relate 
to the terms and conditions of employment or access to public 
services or accommodations within the meaning of section 
102(b)(3) of the Congressional Accountability Act (Public Law 
104-1).

                    DUPLICATION OF FEDERAL PROGRAMS

    Pursuant to clause 3(c)(5) of rule XIII, no provision of 
H.R. 8800 establishes or reauthorizes a program of the Federal 
Government known to be duplicative of another Federal program, 
a program that was included in any report from the Government 
Accountability Office to Congress pursuant to section 21 of 
Public Law 111-139, or a program related to a program 
identified in the most recent Catalog of Federal Domestic 
Assistance.

         CHANGES IN EXISTING LAW MADE BY THE BILL, AS REPORTED

    The committee has taken steps to make available the 
analysis of changes in existing law made by the bill, as 
required by clause 3(e) of rule XIII of the Rules of the House 
of Representatives, and will make the analysis available as 
soon as possible.

                            ADDITIONAL VIEWS

    Following the passage of this year's National Defense 
Authorization Act by the House Armed Services Committee, I 
write to share my additional views and concerns with the bill 
as marked up by the full committee. The National Defense 
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 authorizes significant 
investments in our service members, military families, 
readiness, military construction, shipbuilding, sustainment, 
and the defense industrial base. I appreciate the committee's 
bipartisan work to provide for the common defense and to ensure 
our servicemembers have the support necessary to carry out 
their missions.
    However, I must register serious concern with the direction 
of this bill and the broader defense posture it reflects. The 
bill autho1izes a $1.15 trillion defense topline while Congress 
also plans to advance another $350 billion in defense spending 
through reconciliation, with far too little specificity, 
accountability, or meaningful oversight. At a time when 
taxpayers are being asked to support unprecedented levels of 
defense spending, it is irresponsible for Congress to provide 
the Department with hundreds of billions of additional dollars 
while failing to demand basic discipline over costly nuclear 
modernization programs, politicization of the Department of 
Defense, and the executive branch's use of military force 
without meaningful congressional authorization. I am also 
disappointed that the committee failed to adopt basic 
guardrails for commercial data centers on milita1y 
installations. These shortcomings should be corrected before 
this bill becomes law.

            FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY AND TOPLINE ACCOUNTABILITY

    ``An object in motion remains in motion.'' The term is as 
true in government as it is in physics. Year after year, we 
continue to increase our defense spending, reaching ever-higher 
levels. Adjusted for inflation, we are spending an amount 
roughly equal to what we spend in 1943. Such high levels are 
wholly unjustified today, particularly since this 
administration continues to claim, however unbelievable it may 
be, that we are not at war even as it requests ever larger 
budgets.
    I remain deeply concerned with the defense topline. As this 
administration defunds humanitarian assistance programs, 
dismantles our education system, undermines access to 
healthcare, and chips away at hard-earned public benefits in 
the name of cost savings, the boulder of defense spending 
continues to roll down the hill, picking up speed as it goes, 
regardless of the damage it may cause. It is time for Congress 
to act: to cut wasteful defense spending, impose meaningful 
oversight, and reassert its responsibility to ensure that our 
defense budget is reasonable, accountable, and aligned with the 
needs of the American people.
    A larger defense budget, standing alone, is not a strategy. 
It can mask mismanagement, reward cost growth, and allow 
troubled programs to continue without the discipline that 
Congress should demand. At a time when families across the 
country are asked to make difficult choices, Congress should 
not authorize enormous defense increases without a clear 
showing that every dollar is necessary, executable, and tied to 
real national security outcomes.
    However Sisyphean may seem, it's time for us to push the 
boulder back up the Hill and restore balance. It's time to 
restore true congressional oversight. We cannot keep funding 
ever larger defense budgets with less oversight and be 
surprised when the president takes advantage of it. The first 
step to restoring that balance is for Congress to reclaim its 
constitutional role: demanding transparency before authorizing 
new spending, requiring accountability before expanding failed 
programs, and insisting that no administration, regardless of 
party, may use the military or the public purse without 
meaningful congressional scrutiny.

                   OVERSIGHT AND ACCOUNTABILITY WINS

    Although I remain concerned with the overall direction of 
this bill, I appreciate that several oversight and 
accountability provisions were accepted. These provisions do 
not cure the larger flaws in the bill, but they are meaningful 
steps toward better congressional oversight and a more 
responsible defense enterprise.
    I am encouraged that the bill includes important reforms to 
strengthen cost-growth accountability, including improvements 
to Nunn-McCurdy oversight and additional reporting on NNSA 
cost-growth compliance. It also includes F-35 accountability 
provisions requiring greater scrutiny of multiyear procurement 
savings and a reset plan for the F-35 global sustainment spares 
backlog. I am also pleased that the committee accepted 
provisions related to V-22 Osprey safety oversight, domestic 
manufacturing requirements for shipbuilding programs, limits on 
Jones Act waivers involving foreign entities of concern, 
shipyard workforce concerns, and contractor progress payment 
protection. I am proud to have joined my colleagues in adding 
an amendment that would improve the Departments Right to Repair 
by taking meaningful steps toward improving sustainment 
oversight, technical-data access, and the Department's ability 
to repair and maintain the systems it buys. These wins should 
be built upon, not treated as a substitute for the broader 
accountability this bill still lacks.
    I am proud of my amendment to ensure that the Department of 
Defense can hold defense contractors accountable for poor 
performance. However, I am concerned that a provision included 
in the original bill would have effectively given defense 
contractors a veto over their own punishment. Whether the issue 
is price-gouging, poor performance, or the misallocation of 
taxpayer funds, the Department needs more tools to hold 
contractors accountable, not fewer.

                         NUCLEAR MODERNIZATION

    As I noted in my additional views last year, I continue to 
have grave concerns about the direction of the United States' 
nuclear enterprise. When Congress considers weapons of this 
destructive power, our decisions must be guided by strategic 
need, fiscal reality, risk reduction, and constitutional 
oversight. This bill again fails to demand sufficient scrutiny 
of nuclear modernization plans that are growing more expensive, 
more difficult to execute, and less clearly connected to 
today's security environment.
    For another year, the committee declined to provide the 
Department of Defense with flexibility on the statutory 
requirement to maintain a fixed number of intercontinental 
ballistic missiles. A rigid requirement to keep 400 ICBMs 
deployed and available is not a substitute for analysis. It 
deprives the President and the Department of the flexibility 
needed to adapt nuclear posture to evolving threats, arms 
control opportunities, resource constraints, and the 
demonstrated survivability of the sea-based and bomber legs of 
the triad. Congress should ask what force is necessarily to 
deter adversaries, not preserve an arbitrary number because it 
has become politically difficult to revisit.
    The Sentinel Intercontinental Ballistic Missile program and 
the plutonium modernization program remain clear examples of 
why this oversight is necessary. Sentinel has already 
experienced extraordinary cost growth and schedule pressure, 
yet Congress continues to act as though continuing the program 
unchanged is the only acceptable option. NNSA has also 
repeatedly acknowledged the difficulty of meeting statutory pit 
production requirements, and independent reviews have raised 
serious concerns about costs, schedules, and execution. 
Congress should require credible life-cycle cost estimates, 
integrated schedules, and a full comparison of alternatives, 
including reuse and refurbishment of existing pits where 
technically viable.
    I am also concerned by continued support for the nuclear 
sea-launched cruise missile, tactical nuclear capabilities, 
low-yield nuclear options, potential nuclear-armed hypersonic 
systems, explosive nuclear testing, and expansive missile 
defense concepts that could increase strategic instability. 
Congress should focus on reducing nuclear risks, preserving 
channels for strategic stability, and avoiding costly programs 
that invite arms racing without making the American people 
safer. As I wrote in a journal article earlier this year, 
``Congress may have enabled arms races in the past, but a 
reinvigorated Congress has the authority and responsibility to 
reduce the risk from nuclear weapons. It's time we started 
acting like it.''.

     POLITICIZATION OF THE MILITARY AND DEPARTMENT OF WAR RENAMING

    I strongly object to the committee's decision to adopt 
language deeming references to the Department of Defense and 
Secretary of Defense as references to the Department of War and 
Secretary of War. The name Department of Defense reflects the 
proper purpose of the institution: to defend the United States, 
uphold the Constitution, and protect the American people under 
civilian control. Changing that name does nothing to improve 
readiness, strengthen deterrence, support servicemembers, or 
repair the defense industrial base.
    Instead, this proposal is a costly and disruptive act of 
political symbolism. It would create administrative confusion 
across law, regulation, maps, records, contracts, forms, 
publications, information systems, signage, and official 
communications. More importantly, it sends the wrong message 
about the role of the United States military. Our military 
exists to defend the nation, not to serve as a political 
instrument or a branding opportunity for any administration. 
Congress has a duty to guard against the politicization of the 
armed forces and to preserve the professional, nonpartisan 
character of military service.

                      MILITARY INSTALLATION NAMES

    By contrast, I was pleased that the Committee adopted 
language requiring military installations to be renamed in a 
manner that better reflects American values and honors the 
right people. This is a modest but important victory. Congress 
should not allow any administration to rewrite military history 
at will, restore honors to Confederate generals who betrayed 
the United States, or disregard the process Congress 
established to ensure that our military installations reflect 
the best of our country.
    Names such as Fort Liberty, Fort Moore, Fort Cavazos, Fort 
Gregg-Adams, Fort Johnson, Fort Novosel, Fort Barfoot, and Fort 
Walker honor service, sacrifice, and values worthy of emulation 
by the men and women who wear the uniform. The names of our 
military installations should inspire servicemembers, families, 
and communities.

          DATA CENTERS ON DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE INSTALLATIONS

    I am disappointed that the committee rejected an amendment 
to establish basic oversight for commercial data centers on 
Department of Defense installations. Data centers are becoming 
critical infrastructure, but they also require enormous amounts 
of power, water, land, security, and infrastructure support. 
When such facilities are placed on or near military 
installations, Congress has a responsibility to ensure they do 
not undermine readiness, training, installation resilience, or 
community quality of life.
    The amendment would have required the Secretary of Defense 
to certify, before entering into an agreement for the 
construction or operation of a commercial data center, that the 
facility had a clear military purpose and posed no risk to 
national defense. It would have required the Department to 
assess costs, continuity of operations, energy supply, water 
consumption, sound and light pollution, encroachment on 
training and operations, physical security, supply chain risks, 
personnel security, and the ability of surrounding communities 
to raise concerns. These are not unreasonable requirements. No 
installation should be asked to trade readiness, energy 
resilience, water security, or future mission needs for opaque 
commercial arrangements.

                        CONGRESSIONAL WAR POWERS

    Finally, I am deeply concerned that this bill does not do 
enough to reassert Congress's constitutional role over 
decisions to use military force. The Constitution gives 
Congress the power to declare war, raise and support armies, 
provide and maintain a navy, make rules governing the armed 
forces, and fund military operations. These responsibilities 
are not optional, and they cannot be delegated away because it 
is politically easier to remain silent.
    No administration, of either party, should be permitted to 
place servicemembers in harm's way, risk escalation with 
foreign powers, or initiate sustained hostilities without 
meaningful consultation with Congress and, when required, 
explicit authorization. After-the-fact briefings are not a 
substitute for congressional authorization. This is not a 
partisan issue; it is a constitutional issue. Our 
servicemembers deserve clear legal authority for the missions 
we ask them to execute, and the American people deserve a 
Congress willing to debate and vote on matters of war and 
peace.
    Our decisions should be guided by careful consideration, 
constitutional responsibility, and a commitment to spending 
taxpayer dollars wisely. I will continue to support investments 
that strengthen our servicemembers, improve readiness, rebuild 
the defense industrial base, and protect the United States. But 
I will also continue to oppose policies that waste resources, 
politicize the military, increase nuclear risks, or erode the 
role of Congress in decisions of war and peace. We owe it to 
the American people and to those who se1ve to get this right.
            Sincerely,
                                            John Garamendi,
                                                Member of Congress.
